segments.say: Mira is sitting in a waiting room, in a plastic chair that is a little too small for her. She arrived forty minutes ago for an appointment that was supposed to take five. Her phone died on the bus, the magazines on the table are two years old, and the only thing on the wall is a clock. She has read the poster about hand washing three times, and she is now reading it a fourth.

A quick word about Mira. She's imagined. She's someone we've pictured together, to keep us company through tonight's ideas. She's forty-one, she repairs bicycles for a living, and she's the kind of person who can spend a whole afternoon happily with a stubborn gear cable. Nothing about her is meant to stand for any real person, and nothing in her afternoon is a case study. She's simply here so the ideas have somewhere to land.

Here's the strange part, and perhaps you know it too. Nothing is wrong. Nobody is shouting at Mira, nothing hurts, and she isn't in any danger. And yet the waiting is somehow unpleasant, in a way that is hard to describe. It isn't sadness, and it isn't quite anger. It's a kind of restless emptiness, as if time itself had gone sticky.

Of course, you know exactly what that feeling is. It's boredom. Almost everyone has felt it, in a lecture, in a queue, on a long journey, or on a Sunday afternoon with nothing planned. We tend to treat it as a small thing, a minor annoyance. But when scientists started to look at it closely, they found something much stranger and much more interesting than a minor annoyance.

Here is a line that is often attributed to the French thinker Blaise Pascal, from the seventeenth century. It is usually quoted in a slightly polished form, but the idea is old, and it has been quoted by researchers again and again. Why would sitting quietly in a room be so hard? That is the question we'll follow tonight.

show.text: All of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone.
show.by: a line often attributed to Blaise Pascal, 17th century

segments.say: So here is the question Mira is quietly asking, and maybe you've asked it too. Why does boredom feel so bad? Why can doing nothing feel worse than doing something we don't enjoy? What is happening in the mind and the brain? And what is the feeling actually for?

show.sub: Why does boredom feel so painful?

segments.say: Tonight, we'll start with what boredom really is, and how old the feeling turns out to be. Then we'll visit a famous experiment in which people sat alone in a room with a button that could give them an electric shock. We'll ask why time crawls, what the brain is doing while we wait, and why many researchers now think boredom is a signal rather than a flaw. We'll look at boredom, creativity and meaning, at phones, and at curiosity, and finish with some gentle, research-based ideas.

show.title: Tonight, we'll explore
items: Alone in a room with a shock button

segments.say: Before we begin, a gentle promise. You don't need to do anything with these ideas tonight. You don't need to take notes, and you don't need to stay awake for every minute. If you drift off, that's perfectly fine, and the ideas will still be here tomorrow. For now, we're simply going to be curious about one of the most ordinary feelings there is.
Let's begin with a surprisingly tricky question, which is what we mean by the word. Researchers argued about it for decades, and the answer they've settled on is quite specific.

Most of us would say that boredom is simply a lack of things to do. But that can't be the whole story, because you can be bored in a room full of books, a phone full of games and a calendar full of tasks. And you can be perfectly content doing very little on a lazy morning. So what is boredom, if it isn't having nothing to do?

show.sub: Easy to feel, hard to define

segments.say: In 2012, a team led by the psychologist John Eastwood at York University in Canada, published a careful review in the journal Perspectives on Psychological Science. Their proposal was that boredom is the aversive experience of wanting, but being unable, to engage in satisfying activity. Notice the two halves of that. There is a wanting, and there is a failure to connect.

That wanting is the important part. A bored mind is not a mind at rest. It's a mind that is reaching for something to hold onto, and can't find a grip. That is why boredom feels like itch rather than calm. When nothing is expected of you and you don't want anything, you feel relaxed. When you want to be engaged and can't, you feel bored.

An empty row of plain chairs in a quiet waiting room, with a round clock on the wall above them. Soft daylight falls across the floor, and a lone magazine rests on a small table, untouched, as though the whole afternoon had paused.

A later theory pulled this apart into two ingredients. In 2018, the psychologists Erin Westgate and Timothy Wilson published what they called the MAC model of boredom, where MAC stands for meaning and attentional components. In their view, boredom appears when two things go wrong together, when an activity doesn't fully hold our attention, and when it doesn't feel meaningful or worth doing.

The attention part can go wrong in two directions. If something is too easy, there's nothing to chew on, and the mind drifts. If it's too hard, or too confusing, the mind gives up, and it drifts then too. Boredom lives in both the too-simple and the too-baffling, which already tells us it is more than a shortage of entertainment.

The meaning part is just as interesting. Sorting a pile of old receipts can feel soul-crushing, while sorting a pile of old photographs can feel absorbing, even when the sorting is identical. What changes is whether the activity connects to anything you care about. Boredom, on this view, is partly the mind asking quietly, why am I doing this?

Mira's waiting room fits both ingredients. The poster doesn't hold her attention, because she has read it three times. And the situation doesn't feel meaningful, because she can't do anything useful with the time. She can't leave, she can't plan, and she can't start anything. She is wanting to engage, and has nothing to engage with.

Psychologists have even built questionnaires to measure how easily people get bored. The best known is the Boredom Proneness Scale, created in 1986 by Richard Farmer and Norman Sundberg. It asks people how far they agree with statements such as, it is easy for me to concentrate on my activities, which is scored in reverse, or, many things I have to do are repetitive and monotonous.

Researchers distinguish between state boredom, which is the feeling you have right now in a waiting room, and trait boredom, or boredom proneness, which is how often and how easily a person tends to slip into it. Everyone has the first. People differ quite a lot in the second, and we'll come back to what that difference may mean.

It's also worth saying what boredom isn't. A 2011 study by Elizabeth Goldberg and colleagues, in the Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, found that boredom proneness is distinct from apathy, from anhedonia, which means losing the ability to feel pleasure, and from depression. They overlap, but they are not the same thing. Boredom wants something. Depression often doesn't.

So we have a first idea to carry with us. Boredom is not an absence of stimulation, it's an itch, a wanting to be engaged that nothing satisfies. It is an unpleasant feeling, and as we'll see, that unpleasantness may be the entire point. But first, a question. Is this a modern problem, or have people always felt it?
Next, we'll travel back through history, to a desert monastery, a Danish philosopher and a very Victorian novel, to see how long people have been bored.
